justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish but essentially flat trajectory for the asset in question. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price level, expecting little movement given typical overnight and intraday drift patterns. The one-week estimate nudged slightly higher, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with recent momentum, while the one-month estimate extended that drift further, producing only a marginal gain over the full period. In all three cases, the central tendency was shaped by an assumption of mean-reverting behavior around recent price levels, with no strong directional catalyst assumed to be imminent.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the range is relatively tight because short-term price behavior is somewhat constrained by liquidity and market microstructure. By one week, the interval widens meaningfully as intraweek macro data releases, sentiment shifts, and positioning changes introduce genuine randomness. At one month, the interval roughly doubles relative to the one-week width, consistent with volatility scaling with the square root of time. I also accounted for the possibility of regime shifts — periods where realized volatility spikes well above its recent average — which fattens the tails of the distribution, particularly at the monthly horizon.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharper-than-expected inflation reading or an abrupt tightening signal from a central bank — could produce a swift selloff that breaks below my lower bounds. Geopolitical escalation or a sudden credit event in a systemically important institution would also represent tail risks that my intervals do not fully capture. On the upside, a strongly positive earnings surprise, a pivot signal from monetary authorities, or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices well above my upper bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons where positioning effects have more time to play out.

It is worth being transparent that these forecasts carry inherent model uncertainty beyond the stated confidence intervals. The intervals represent my attempt to quantify known unknowns, but unknown unknowns — structural breaks, flash crashes, or unprecedented policy actions — fall outside what any probabilistic framework can reliably bound. Readers should treat the outer edges of the intervals as approximate rather than precise probability thresholds, and recognize that realized outcomes at the one-month horizon especially may surprise in either direction with greater frequency than a normal distribution would suggest.
